text:
The chair of the National Assembly’s Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee told Iran’s newly appointed ambassador to Korea that the planned expansion of the Cheonghae Unit’s operational area near the Strait of Hormuz is aimed solely at ensuring freedom of navigation, not at joining a military campaign against Tehran.
“The ambassador expressed concern about military deployment in the strait and I made our position clear that this is not the case,” Rep. Song Seog-jun told The Korea Times Wednesday.
Ahmad Erfanian, Iran’s newly appointed ambassador to Korea, paid a courtesy call to Song's office, Monday, and the two exchanged introductory greetings following the ambassador’s appointment and discussed key issues between Korea and Iran.
Song said he sought to ease the ambassador’s concerns. “I told him that this is not an expansion of military deployment. Korea is expanding our role only to the minimum extent necessary to ensure freedom of navigation.”
During their meeting, Song expressed hope for a swift restoration of peace and stability in the Middle East without further conflict, to which Erfanian responded by asking Seoul to play a greater role in bringing the war to an end quickly.
Song referred to Seo Hui, a 10th-century Goryeo civil official who secured territorial concessions from the Khitan empire through negotiation rather than battle. Showing Erfanian a photo of the historical figure, Song said he hoped both sides could find a path to peace through dialogue, in keeping with Seo’s legacy.
“Korea has pursued win-win strategies. Since ancient times, Koreans have achieved peace through mutually acceptable solutions without resorting to fighting,” he told The Korea Times.
The visit comes as the National Assembly prepares to vote on the government’s plan to expand the Cheonghae Unit’s operational area from the Gulf of Aden to waters south of Oman, a move requiring parliamentary approval. The expansion is driven in part by U.S. pressure on allies to help secure the Strait of Hormuz, a focal point of the monthslong war with Iran.
When asked whether Erfanian’s courtesy call to Song was related to the Cheonghae Unit, the Iranian Embassy confirmed only that the ambassador had visited Song.
The Iranian government issued a public warning apparently aimed at Korea’s plan to expand the Cheonghae Unit’s mission closer to the Strait of Hormuz.
In a Nov. 13 post on X, Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei opened with a Korean proverb that cautions against overreach: “ A sparrow that tries to fly after a stork will eventually break its legs .”
He added, “Any direct or indirect involvement in acts of aggression or in inhumane economic terrorism against Iran — including the deployment of naval forces, military and logistical support equipment, and personnel — will be regarded as a hostile and unlawful act amounting to participation in the U.S. aggression against Iran.”
The planned expansion has also drawn criticism within Korea. Some lawmakers from the main opposition People Power Party argue the move amounts to a de facto military deployment, while the minor Rebuilding Korea Party has mounted an all-out campaign against it. Some experts have also expressed concern that an accidental clash could draw Korea into the U.S.-Iran conflict.
Korea Times reporter Kim Bo-kyoung contributed to this article.
